title: Oi Muchim
subtitle: Spicy Korean cucumber salad
excerpt: Salted cucumber is squeezed dry and tossed in a bright dressing of gochugaru, garlic, rice vinegar and sesame oil. This banchan comes together in 15 minutes and pairs with virtually any Korean meal. The salting step is what separates a crisp salad from a watery one.
sourceNotes: Oi muchim is one of the most common summer banchan across Korea, made in every household when cucumbers are abundant and the weather is warm. The technique of salting and squeezing vegetables before seasoning is central to Korean salad-making and applies to many other muchim dishes beyond cucumber.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best eaten within an hour of making. The salad continues to release liquid as it sits.

glossaryTerms.definition: Muchim is a category of Korean side dishes in which ingredients are mixed or tossed with a seasoning mixture. The word means 'to mix' or 'to season'. Muchim dishes can be made with raw vegetables, blanched greens, or cooked ingredients, and the seasoning typically includes some combination of gochugaru, garlic, sesame oil and soy sauce.

Oi is the Korean word for cucumber. Korean cucumbers are thinner and less seedy than the large English varieties commonly found in British supermarkets. English cucumbers work well in this recipe but benefit from having their seeds scraped out before slicing to reduce excess water in the finished dish.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 as a banchan side and takes 15 minutes to prepare, with no cooking required.

Salt the cucumber slices and leave them for 10 minutes, then wring them firmly in a clean tea towel or squeeze them by the handful. You will be surprised how much water comes out. This step cannot be skipped if you want a salad that holds its texture for more than a few minutes.

content.text: Slice the cucumber thinly. Place in a colander or bowl, sprinkle over the salt, toss to coat, and leave for 10 minutes.
Squeeze the cucumber firmly in a clean tea towel or wring by the handful to remove as much liquid as possible. Transfer the squeezed cucumber to a mixing bowl.
Add the gochugaru, rice vinegar, sesame oil, garlic, spring onions and sugar to the bowl.
Taste and adjust. Add more gochugaru for heat, more sugar for sweetness, or more vinegar for sharpness. Serve at once or within an hour. The cucumber softens as it sits in the dressing.
Taste and adjust. Add a little more gochugaru for heat, more rice vinegar for sharpness, or more sugar to balance. Scatter over the sesame seeds and serve.

items.symptom: Salad is watery and the dressing slides off
items.cause: The cucumber was not squeezed firmly enough after salting
items.fix: Go back and squeeze more aggressively. Use a clean tea towel and wring tightly, or press in a sieve with the back of a spoon. The cucumber should feel almost dry.

items.cause: Salt was left on too long or not fully drained before dressing
items.fix: Rinse the salted cucumber briefly under cold water, then squeeze dry before dressing. Reduce the salt to half a teaspoon next time.

items.symptom: The salad loses its crunch quickly on the table
items.cause: Cucumber draws water as it sits in salt
items.fix: Salt and squeeze the cucumber before dressing. Serve within an hour of mixing.

content.text: Oi muchim is a summer staple in Korea. It appears at barbecues, alongside grilled meats, and as a cooling counterpoint to heavier stews. The salad is quick enough to make fresh for each meal. It costs almost nothing and requires no specialist equipment. Many cooks add a tiny splash of fish sauce for depth, but the vegan version here is just as good.
